problem: Prior zero-shot object-goal navigation mostly handles category names, and struggles with language descriptions containing attributes and spatial relations; CLIP is order-agnostic, and LLM/VLM answers are noisy, hallucinated and inconsistent.
motivation: Service robots must follow descriptive instructions such as 'the black chair between the TV and desk' and pick the right instance among several. VLM generative and discriminative answers disagree, so a mechanism that makes them coherent should reduce hallucinated target selection, even for small VLMs.
key_idea: Build a CLIP-based 3D object-centric map for frontier exploration, then verify candidate targets with a VLM using multi-view images, resolving the decision via a Consensus-Game-style generator/discriminator equilibrium search (piKL no-regret).
insight: Spatial relations are delegated to a VLM over top-view plus first-person images, while CLIP handles only the main object. Equilibrium search over sampled generator and discriminator distributions beats a single generator and 5-sample ranking, and the gain is larger for GPT-4o-mini (SR 0.354 vs 0.332 ranking, 0.304 generator), so it even beats GPT-4o generator (0.351). In the object-goal ablation, semantic similarity maps beat the nearest-frontier policy on SPL (0.243 vs 0.264/0.268).
method: 3D object-centric map: Grounding-DINO detection, Mobile-SAM masks and CLIP features per mask, projected with depth and merged by semantic and geometric similarity into object nodes (ConceptGraphs-style).

2D exploration map: 3D points are projected to obstacle/explored channels, frontiers are extracted by contour and dilation and clustered; FMM planning with a local policy; an LLM chooses up/down stairs when the floor is exhausted.

Frontier scoring: cost-utility geometry score plus object-level CLIP similarity map and image-level CLIP similarity map, selected with score bounds B=[0.22,0.26] (object sim > B_sup, else image sim > B_inf, else geometry).
Language parsing: an LLM extracts the main goal with attributes and drops spatial relations; a candidate list with approach-to-verify handles CLIP's view inconsistency.

Multi-view candidate verification: top-view and first-person images of each candidate, extracted from the 3D map, are given to the VLM with the description; if none match, all are rejected and exploration continues.

Vision-language equilibrium search: the generator pi_G (choose ID over all candidates) and discriminator pi_D (is this candidate correct) are initialized from 5 VLM samples; piKL updates with KL regularization (eta=lambda=0.1, T=1.0) converge to consensus policies; the final target is chosen from them.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o-2024-05-13 / GPT-4o-mini (frozen) for identification, plus Grounding-DINO, Mobile-SAM, CLIP; an LLM for parsing and stairs
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D 480x640 plus odometry/pose, and goal category or language description
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move_forward 25 cm, turn_left/right 30°, look_up/down 30°, stop; 500 step limit
setting.privileged: none (pose given in sim; lidar+GMapping localization on real robot)

numbers.eval_set_note: 316 episodes extracted from Goat-bench with language descriptions (split not specified)

numbers_note: GOAT-Bench split is not stated in the text; 'val' is assumed. Only the six-category HM3D ObjectNav validation was reported, not the official challenge.
results: On HM3D ObjectNav, VLN-Game gets SR 0.613 / SPL 0.268, beating InstructNav (0.580 SR, 0.209 SPL) and VLFM (0.525 SR), though VLFM keeps higher SPL (0.304). On 316 GOAT language-goal episodes, VLN-Game with GPT-4o reaches SR 0.367, above VLN-Ranking (0.364) and Generator (0.351), while GPT-4o-mini VLN-Game (0.354) beats GPT-4o Generator.
limitations: CLIP similarity is inconsistent across views and misses many open-vocabulary targets, limiting detection and recall.
Language-goal gains are small (about +0.3 to +2 SR points over ranking) on a small 316-episode subset, and use repeated GPT-4o API sampling (5 samples, iterative updates), which costs latency.
Real-world evaluation is qualitative only, with one target per instruction and no quantitative metrics.
